title: I let a bot play my incremental game to balance it. Here’s what it caught and what it missed
author: Noah__1302
selftext:
I’m building a small incremental game where you play a black hole that grows from dust up to the universe. The code is almost entirely written with Claude (Opus 5.5, mostly extra high). I set the direction and did the playtesting myself. There are no art asset files: the planets and the hole are procedural shaders, the sounds and music come from a Python script, and the UI icons are vector shapes in code.

The hard part was and is balancing. I can’t playtest for hours on end, so I had Claude build a bot that plays the first tiers headless and measures how long each one takes. Target times live in a JSON file, and the bot should need about 80% of them, since humans are slower. What it caught: stretches where nothing was affordable for two runs in a row. What it missed: how the game actually feels. For that I had to play it myself. 

I’m curious how you handle this. Do you test balancing with simulation, with real players, or by feel? And where do you use AI bots without them taking the fun out of the design?

Second question, since I’m still looking for playtesters: what’s worked for you in getting people to test an unfinished game? I’ve had a hard time getting anyone to try it so far.

It’s up on itch io as a browser build if anyone wants to poke at it.

comments.author: PositiveScarcity8909
comments.body:
AI is good at managing data, not at sourcing data.

Take the measurements yourself and then let it use those to arrive to conclusions that you may have missed.

Claude measured winrates for my game and divided them by 20% winrate increments with the "strong" player at 80% winrate.

But I know a strong player will have 99% winrate and the average player will be at around 80-90% so the data made no sense.

I had to hard force the data for Claude to be useful at all.

replies.author: Noah__1302
replies.body: Thanks, that’s a useful warning. My bot measures time to reach each tier and dry streaks, not win rates, so binning like that wouldn’t apply, but I’ll check it against what I actually see when I play. Did you end up fixing the data by hand, or did you drop the bot entirely?

replies.author: PositiveScarcity8909
replies.body:
I fixed the data by hand and let Claude do the calculations.

I've come to find that you need to be very specific with everything you say.

Another example was that I used to add examples to a prompt as a way for Claude to understand what I was explaining better, a very human thing to do. 

But Claude took this as a Bible and pasted that example as if it was a decided thing into every iteration of the design document. 

Much later and one of my mechanics was not implemented because it would clash with the dumb example I made 2 weeks ago

comments.author: PersonOfInterest007
comments.body: I’d be cautious about doing game balancing using only an agent. Humans may use a completely different style, or set of styles. You can use the agent to find blocking problems etc, but balancing is largely about making a game feel good to actual players.

replies.author: Noah__1302
replies.body: Agreed, and that’s the part I keep running into. My bot can show blocking points and dead stretches, but it never hesitates the way a player does. So I use it to find problems, then I play through myself to judge the feel.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Can one measure fun? 😜 That would be useful. 
Agreeing with you here, better to be the player with a lot of playtime in your own game.

comments.author: thatguywithimpact
comments.body:
I had a very long balancing runs where AI plays and balances levels at the same time according to my design (not sure how efficient that was) but results were amazing. I'm not sure how long it would take for me to balance this well without AI or if I could make such a high quality balance at all. 

But I still have to play through the whole game and I caught many things that AI didn't and I still have to play to the end. But with challenging game I designed it's not easy lol I know it's beatable by design and by bot, but still

replies.author: Noah__1302
replies.body: Same experience here: the bot found pacing gaps I’d never have spotted by reading the formulas, but it still couldn’t tell me whether a stretch felt boring. Playing the whole thing yourself is the part no agent replaces. Glad your challenge still lands for humans, that’s the hard bit to get right.
